summary: This document explains authenticated denial of existence in DNS, which lets a resolver verify that a name does not exist or that a record type is missing. It describes how DNSSEC negative responses work and compares the available approaches.

eli5.summary: If you ask a library for a book it does not have, how do you know the librarian is telling the truth? This explains how DNS can prove that something is truly not there.

questions: how does dnssec prove a name does not exist
what is authenticated denial of existence
subtitle: How DNSSEC proves that a domain name or record type does not exist.

tldr.problem: DNS responses can be forged. When a resolver asks for a domain name that does not exist, how can it be sure the 'no such domain' answer is genuine and not spoofed?
tldr.mechanism: DNSSEC uses NSEC or NSEC3 records, which define intervals between existing names in the zone. A signed NSEC record proves that a queried name falls in a gap between two existing names, so it cannot exist. For asking about missing record types, the NSEC type bitmap shows which types exist at a name, proving the absence of others.
tldr.outcome: DNSSEC now provides authenticated denial of existence, so a resolver can cryptographically verify that a domain name or record type is genuinely absent, not spoofed.

today: RFC 7129 is an informational explanation of DNSSEC authenticated denial of existence. NSEC is still used, but NSEC3 is now standard for larger zones due to better privacy and operational properties. The techniques explained here remain the foundation for all DNSSEC negative response handling.

sections.title: The Problem of Proving Nonexistence
sections.content:
In plain DNS, a server answers 'does not exist' to a query with a simple status code. But a man-in-the-middle attacker can send a forged 'does not exist' response just as easily as a real one. The DNS packet header is not signed, so the resolver has no way to know whether the answer is authentic.

DNSSEC solves this by signing negative responses. But what do you sign when there is nothing to sign? The solution is to sign records that describe intervals: if we say 'between these two real names there is nothing', and that record is signed, then we have cryptographically proven that any name in between does not exist.
sections.eli5: A forged 'not found' answer is as easy to fake as a real one. DNSSEC signs a record that says 'between Alice and Dan, there is nothing', so if Bob falls in that gap, Bob must not exist.

sections.title: NSEC: Signed Name Intervals
sections.content:
NSEC (Next Secure) records form a chain through all names in a sorted zone. Each NSEC record points to the next name and lists the record types that exist at the current name. For example, the NSEC for 'alice.example.com' might say 'the next name is bob.example.com, and alice has A and MX records'. A resolver can then prove 'b.example.com does not exist' by finding the NSEC for alice (which says the next name is bob) and checking that b falls alphabetically between alice and bob.

NSEC also serves a second purpose: the type bitmap in the NSEC record shows which record types are defined for a name. So if a resolver asks for 'alice.example.com AAAA' and the NSEC record shows alice only has A and MX types, the resolver can prove that AAAA does not exist at alice without needing a separate denial record.
sections.eli5: NSEC records are like a chain of names in alphabetical order. Each one says 'I am alice, the next is bob, and I have A and MX records'. From this chain, you can prove a missing name or missing record type.

sections.title: The Drawbacks of NSEC and the Rise of NSEC3
sections.content:
NSEC has two problems. First, the chain of names is in alphabetical order, so an attacker can walk through the entire zone by following the chain from one name to the next, defeating the confidentiality of the zone contents. Second, every name in a large zone needs an NSEC record and signature, which means the signed zone is much larger than the unsigned zone. For delegation-centric zones (zones with many delegations to other zones), this overhead can be significant.

NSEC3 solves these problems by hashing the zone names. Instead of 'alice.example.com', the NSEC3 chain uses hashes of names in Base32 encoding, making it much harder to recover the original names. NSEC3 also supports Opt-Out: names that are delegations to unsigned zones do not need NSEC3 records, which means operators can incrementally deploy DNSSEC without signing the entire zone upfront.
sections.eli5: NSEC leaks the zone contents (you can list all names by following the chain), and it takes space for every name. NSEC3 hashes the names so you cannot see them, and lets you skip unsigned delegations.

sections.title: NSEC3 Details and Complexity
sections.content:
NSEC3 records store hashes of names (using SHA1 with configurable iterations and a salt to prevent pre-computation). The NSEC3 chain is sorted by hash value instead of alphabetical order, which flattens the zone structure. To prove denial of existence in NSEC3, a resolver must verify two records: one that matches the closest existing parent name of the query name (to show it exists), and one that covers the 'next closer name' (to show that the query name is not one level deeper). Wildcards and CNAME records add further complexity: the resolver must verify that wildcard expansion was not applicable.

The zone operator stores NSEC3 parameters (hash iterations, salt) in an NSEC3PARAM record at the zone apex so secondaries and validators know how to validate responses. Despite the additional complexity, NSEC3 has become the standard for larger or sensitive zones because it protects zone privacy while supporting incremental deployment.
sections.eli5: NSEC3 hashes the names and uses a special trick (closest encloser proof) to check nonexistence. It is more complex than NSEC but solves the privacy and space problems.

sections.title: Wildcards and Denial of Existence
sections.content:
Wildcards (like *.example.com) complicate denial of existence. If a resolver queries for a name that does not exist but matches a wildcard, the server answers with the wildcard expansion (e.g., answering 'z.example.com' with data from the wildcard). To prove that an answer came from a wildcard and not from a literal name, DNSSEC requires the server to include an NSEC (or NSEC3) record in the response that proves no direct match exists. Without this record, an attacker could modify the answer packet to make it look like a real (but different) name was returned.

CNAME records (aliases) can also be wildcard-expanded in chains, requiring multiple NSEC records in a response to prove that each step in the CNAME chain was from a wildcard and not a literal name. The DNS specification calls this 'following the lookup algorithm', and DNSSEC must communicate that each step was legitimate by including the appropriate denial records.
sections.eli5: Wildcards let you say 'anything at this level gets this answer'. But you have to prove with NSEC that the answer really came from the wildcard, not from a fake name.
